title: Back Squat
summary: The barbell squat with the bar on the upper back: quads are the main mover, with glutes and adductors helping. One of the most loadable and most fatiguing lifts in the library.

equipment_needs.text: Needs: barbell (Olympic bar); weight plates; rack with J-hooks (power rack, squat stands or bench uprights).

muscles.why: The quads straighten the knee out of a deep knee bend. The vasti (the three single-joint heads) are rated 1; the rectus femoris crosses the hip too, shortening at the hip as it lengthens at the knee, so it changes length little and is rated 0.4.

region_notes.text: Squats did not grow the rectus femoris in a 10-week MRI study, and leg extensions grew it where Smith-machine squats did not.

muscles.why: The glutes extend the hip out of the hole; they work hardest when you squat deep.
The adductor magnus is a strong hip extender in a deep squat.
The spinal erectors hold the torso against the bar's weight; isometric work.
Hip abductors keep the knees tracking over the toes: minor.
The abs brace the trunk, but rated below the counting floor (0.15).

setup.text: Set the bar in a rack at mid-chest height and the safety arms just below your bottom position.
Bar on the upper traps (high bar) or across the rear delts (low bar); grip just outside the shoulders.
Walk it out in two or three short steps; feet about shoulder width, toes slightly out.
Breathe in, brace your abs and keep the brace for the whole rep.

form_cues.why: A fresh brace each rep keeps the trunk stiff under the bar.

form_cues.cue: Sit down between your hips with knees tracking toes
form_cues.why: Knees tracking over the toes lets the hips sit down between the legs.

form_cues.cue: Drive up through the whole foot
form_cues.why: Pressing through the whole foot keeps the bar over mid-foot, where you are balanced.

form_cues.cue: Depth matters. Deep squats build more quad and glute than half reps.
form_cues.why: Full-depth squats grew the glutes and adductors more than half squats in an MRI study; quad growth was similar.
Any drift forward or back adds load to the lower back.

bias_tweaks.change: Squat to full depth (hip crease below the knee)
bias_tweaks.effect: More glute and adductor growth than half squats; similar quad growth.
bias_tweaks.caveat: One 10-week study in 17 men. Go as deep as you can with a neutral back.

bias_tweaks.change: High bar, upright torso, knees forward
bias_tweaks.effect: More knee bend, so the quads do a larger share.
bias_tweaks.caveat: Depends a lot on your build.

bias_tweaks.change: Low bar, wider stance, more forward lean
bias_tweaks.effect: More hip bend, so more glute and back work and usually more load.
bias_tweaks.caveat: More spinal loading, and harder to learn.

bias_tweaks.change: Pause one second at the bottom
bias_tweaks.effect: Removes the bounce, builds control at depth; costs load.
bias_tweaks.caveat: Tempo itself makes little difference to growth in normal ranges.

mistakes.text: Letting the knees cave in on the way up.
mistakes.fix: Push the knees out over the toes on the way up; lighten the load if they still cave.

mistakes.text: Losing depth as the weight goes up.
mistakes.fix: Use the same depth every rep so your logged loads compare.
Shift the weight to mid-foot; lifting shoes or small plates under the heels help some lifters.

mistakes.text: Hips shooting up first out of the hole.
mistakes.fix: Drive the chest and hips up together.

misconceptions.myth: Squats are the best quad builder.
misconceptions.reality: Squats grew the vasti well but not the rectus femoris; leg extensions filled that gap in two studies.

misconceptions.myth: Squats are bad for your knees if they go past your toes.
misconceptions.reality: Knees travelling forward is a normal part of a deep squat. Use the depth and stance you can train comfortably.

misconceptions.myth: Every set has to go to failure to grow.
misconceptions.reality: Stopping a few reps short gave similar growth to failure in a meta-analysis; growth tends to rise as sets get closer to failure, but the exact curve is uncertain.

lower_risk.text: Ramp up before your first working set. For primary lifts the app suggests 50% x 8, 70% x 4 and 85% x 2 when the first working load is 60 kg or more, and 50% x 8 then 75% x 3 below that.
lower_risk.note: High-load warm-ups improved strength performance in a systematic review; the percentages are coaching convention.

lower_risk.text: Add load in small steps. The app suggests a heavier load only when the jump is 5% or less; otherwise it adds a rep first, up to 2 past the top of the range. Default steps for this equipment are 2.5 kg or 5 lb; your gym profile can replace them.
Aim for about 3 reps in reserve in the 6-10 rep range. Keep heavy squat sets a few reps short of failure, and always squat with safeties set or a spotter.
Squat inside a rack with the safety arms just below your bottom position, so a missed rep can be set down. Use collars.
Control the descent; don't drop and bounce out of the hole.
Pick a variation, range and setup you can train comfortably.

alternatives.why: Machine-guided quad work with no bar on the spine.
Heavy quad training with far less whole-body fatigue.
Fixed bar path, easier to learn, still loadable.
Needs one dumbbell; upright and easy to learn, but loading is limited.
Grew the rectus femoris where squats did not.
One leg at a time, no heavy bar on the back, more glute work.

notes: Squat-depth results come from one 10-week MRI study in 17 men.
Ratings and display bands are the library model (main >= 0.75, helper 0.4 to < 0.75, minor 0.25 to < 0.4, not counted < 0.25).
Technique and load management only. This page makes no medical or injury claims.
